title: Outcome Monitors: Recovery Affordances for Silent Tool Failures
authors: Sugam Panthi, Rabab Abdelfattah
central_claim: Template-mined outcome contracts (echo, positivity, categorical domain, affine, date ordering) from nominal traces flag silent tool failures; receipts naming recovery tools lift ToolMaze completion 10.9% to 28.1%; detection falls to ~46% outside the mined vocabulary. Same source as RESEARCH.md C11.
cite_claim: Contracts are mined with zero model calls from task-disjoint nominal traces (15,041 invariants from 400 workflows, five-fold cross-fitted); an invariant is kept only if it holds on every training sample; FP 1.39% per outcome on synthetic clean traffic and 0.80% on 6,860 organic held-out responses; recall 83% for structured values but 22% for corruption inside plausible strings.
location: Sec. 3.2 (Alg. 2), Sec. 3.3, Sec. 5.5, App. E, App. G, App. O, Sec. 6
quote: An invariant must hold on every training sample and meet its class-specific support minimum.
relevance: Closest prior art for inferring fiks contracts from v1 traffic and the source of C11. Gives an implementable algorithm, cross-fitting protocol and FP numbers to replicate. It also warns that miner and injector may be aligned (Sec. 6), which applies directly to fiks's seeded D1-D5.

title: Contract2Tool: Learning Preconditions and Effects for Reliable Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
authors: Rahul Suresh Babu, Laxmipriya Ganesh Iyer
central_claim: LLMs generate tool contracts (requires/produces/risk) from name, metadata, schema, documentation and/or execution traces; trace and hybrid contracts recover the gold causal frontier exactly on a synthetic 100-tool registry.
cite_claim: Learned contracts drive tool filtering with 0.980 downstream success vs 0.990 for gold contracts; trace-derived contracts expose 0.000 extra tools in the filter-oracle test vs 0.081-0.396 for documentation-only contracts; the registry is synthetic and execution is mocked.
location: Sec. IV-D, VII-C (Table IV), VII-D, IX
quote: Successful traces reveal produced state variables through before-and-after state differences.
relevance: LLM-based contract inference for agent tools using traces. It targets preconditions and effects for tool selection, not output-correctness invariants. Evidence that traces beat documentation as an evidence source.

title: Symbolic Temporal Supervision of LLM Agents Using Contracts
authors: Yifeng Xiao, Pierluigi Nuzzo
central_claim: Assume-guarantee contracts in (arithmetic) LTLf over tool-call predicates, compiled to DFAs, supervise agents at runtime; contracts are mostly hand-written or LLM-lifted from SOPs, with a trace-learned variant for AgentDojo.
cite_claim: On replayed SOPBench traces the false-positive rate stayed below 1% for 19 of 23 models (max 4.5%); trace-learned contracts lowered AgentDojo attack success to 0.79% at 72.6% utility; the framework only enforces what the tool-call structure exposes.
quote: enforces only what the tool-call structure exposes
relevance: Temporal contracts over tool calls are the natural formalism for fiks read-after-write postconditions. Its own limitation (no content-level semantics) is the gap fiks's value invariants fill.

title: AgentSpec: Customizable Runtime Enforcement for Safe and Reliable LLM Agents
authors: Haoyu Wang, Christopher M. Poskitt, Jun Sun
central_claim: A DSL of trigger-predicate-enforcement rules for runtime enforcement on LLM agents; LLM-generated rules reach high precision but lower recall.
cite_claim: Rules generated by OpenAI o1 achieve 95.56% precision and 70.96% recall for embodied agents.
quote: achieve a precision of 95.56% and recall of 70.96% for embodied agents
relevance: Shows the precision-high, recall-limited profile of LLM-generated runtime rules. That is the same trade-off fiks faces if an LLM proposes contracts. It is a safety domain, not tool-output correctness.

title: LLM-Based Invariant Testing for Software Functional Bugs (Lisa)
authors: Ruogu Yang, Yifeng He, Yundi Xu, Yuqing Wei, Hao Chen
venue_or_publisher: arXiv 2607.18711 (extended version of an ISSRE 2026 paper)
central_claim: Daikon candidates filtered by documentation plus LLM-extracted documented invariants find more functional bugs than Daikon alone or fuzzing.
cite_claim: Lisa detected 12/25 re-introduced historical bugs vs 5/25 for a Daikon-only variant, 3 for CITYWALK and 2 for OSS-Fuzz; Daikon-only introduces substantial noise; Daikon invariants capture the current version and suit regression testing.
location: Sec. III-G1, V-D (Table VI), VI-B, VII-C
quote: better suited for generating regression tests rather than detecting functional bugs
relevance: A recent hybrid design for fiks: mine candidates dynamically and keep only those consistent with documentation. Also the clearest statement that trace-mined invariants are regression oracles. No FP rate is reported.

title: AGORA: Automated Generation of Test Oracles for REST APIs
authors: Juan C. Alonso, Sergio Segura, Antonio Ruiz-Cortes
central_claim: Black-box likely-invariant inference over REST request/response traffic (extended Daikon, up to 105 invariant types) yields precise test oracles.
cite_claim: AGORA achieved 81.2% total precision on 11 operations from 7 industrial APIs, detected about 6 in 10 seeded output errors, and revealed 11 bugs in APIs with millions of users.
quote: AGORA achieved a total precision of 81.2% when tested on a dataset of 11 operations from 7 industrial APIs
relevance: The canonical technique for inferring response invariants from API traffic. It is the strongest runnable baseline for fiks contract inference (via Beet + modified Daikon).

title: Test oracle generation for REST APIs (AGORA+)
authors: Juan C. Alonso, Michael D. Ernst, Sergio Segura, Antonio Ruiz-Cortes
central_claim: AGORA+ detects 106 REST invariant types and emits executable Postman assertions (PostmanAssertify).
cite_claim: AGORA+ achieved 80% precision on 25 operations from 20 industrial APIs, identified 48% of systematically seeded output errors, and uncovered 32 bugs in popular APIs.
quote: It also identified 48% of errors systematically seeded in the outputs of the APIs under test.
relevance: Gives a published precision (~80%) and seeded-error recall (48%) for traffic-mined API invariants. These are calibration points for any fiks inferred-contract result. Note that 20% imprecision per invariant is far from an acceptable per-receipt FP rate.

title: Beet: instrumenter for Daikon over OpenAPI request/response traces (AGORA+)
authors: ISA Group, University of Seville
central_claim: Converts an OpenAPI spec plus a CSV of requests/responses to Daikon declaration and trace files; the modified Daikon runs from a Docker image; invariants need developer confirmation.
cite_claim: Inputs are an OpenAPI spec and a CSV of request parameters plus JSON responses. The license is GPL-3.0, and the README says arithmetic comparison invariants are the main false-positive source.
quote: converts any OpenAPI specification and a collection of API requests (and responses)
relevance: Makes AGORA+ a baseline fiks can actually run, from fiks's recorded v1 upstream exchanges converted to CSV, run as a separate GPL process. The FP-source note informs template choice. [verify exact README wording on arithmetic-comparison FPs]

title: SATORI: Static Test Oracle Generation for REST APIs
authors: Juan C. Alonso, Alberto Martin-Lopez, Sergio Segura, Gabriele Bavota, Antonio Ruiz-Cortes
central_claim: An LLM reads only the OpenAPI specification (no execution) and generates response oracles; it is complementary to dynamic AGORA+.
cite_claim: SATORI F1 74.3% vs 69.3% for AGORA+ on comparable oracle types (17 operations, 12 industrial APIs); together they found 90% of ground-truth oracles; 18 bugs found.
quote: together, SATORI and AGORA+ found 90% of the oracles in our annotated ground-truth dataset
relevance: Evidence that static (spec/description) and dynamic (traffic) inference are complementary. This motivates a hybrid fiks inferer that uses MCP tool descriptions/outputSchema [C26] plus v1 traffic.

title: MASTOR: A Multi-Agent Approach to Semantic Test Oracle Generation for RESTful APIs
authors: Sida Deng, Rubing Huang, Zhenzhen Yang, Man Zhang, Xuan Xie, Rongcun Wang
central_claim: Multi-agent LLM oracle generation from implementation source code beats direct prompting and SATORI on mutation score.
cite_claim: 75.4% average mutation score with 10,022 oracles on 13 open-source APIs (296 operations); on 50 operations 69.9% vs 39.8% (direct prompting) and 20.5% (SATORI). Uses mutation score instead of precision because no complete ground-truth oracle set exists.
location: Abstract; Sec. evaluation metrics; Related work (AGORA+)
quote: AGORA+ derived its constraints from observed executions; therefore, the coverage of inferred properties depended on the diversity of available traces.
relevance: Shows that oracle-quality numbers in this literature use incompatible metrics (precision vs F1 vs mutation score). fiks must report per-receipt FP on clean traffic, not mutation score, because a false receipt is what an agent pays for.

title: RESTOR: Automated Test Oracle Generation for RESTful APIs via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Xun Zhou, Zhen Dong, Mingyu Ren, Qiang Li, JunJie Li, Sifan Wang, Xiaolong Yu, Chaofeng Sha, Xin Peng
central_claim: A small LLM fine-tuned with GRPO produces assertions from a single request-response pair, rewarded for stable fields and avoiding dynamic noise; deployed at ByteDance.
cite_claim: F1 85.42% in key-field identification over 2,300+ traces from 246 services; production adoption of generated tests rose from 74.1% to over 96%.
quote: executable test assertions from a single observed request-response pair
relevance: Industrial evidence that separating stable from dynamic (noisy) fields is the crux of oracle generation from traffic. That maps directly onto fiks equalsUpstream/notNull selection.

title: Metamorphic Testing of RESTful Web APIs
authors: Sergio Segura, Jose A. Parejo, Javier Troya, Antonio Ruiz-Cortes
central_claim: Metamorphic relations over multiple API calls (e.g. a filtered search returns a subset) work around the oracle problem for web APIs; six output patterns (MROPs) instantiate concrete relations.
cite_claim: Six Metamorphic Relation Output Patterns were defined; 60 metamorphic relations were identified in the Spotify and YouTube APIs; evaluation used seeded and real faults.
location: Abstract (via Universidad de Sevilla repository record) [verify wording against full text]
quote: Metamorphic Testing of RESTful Web APIs
relevance: Cross-call relations, such as search vs get_product consistency or paging-union equals unpaged results, catch D4-style pagination drift without knowing the right answer. These are relations fiks's single-call vocabulary lacks.

title: Can Large Language Models Discover Metamorphic Relations? A Large-Scale Empirical Study
authors: Jiaming Zhang, Chang-ai Sun, Huai Liu, Sijin Dong
central_claim: LLMs propose metamorphic relation candidates of which a third to a half are valid, mostly novel.
cite_claim: On 37 SUTs, 34.03% (gpt-3.5) and 50.04% (gpt-4) of MR candidates were valid; 82.81% and 88.22% of valid MRs were new.
quote: 34.03% and 50.04% of all MRCs are identified as the MRs valid for the corresponding SUT
relevance: If fiks uses an LLM to propose cross-call relations, half or more of the candidates will be invalid, so a traffic-based falsification filter is mandatory.

title: Can Large Language Models Transform Natural Language Intent into Formal Method Postconditions? (nl2postcond)
authors: Madeline Endres, Sarah Fakhoury, Saikat Chakraborty, Shuvendu K. Lahiri
central_claim: LLMs turn natural-language intent into checkable postconditions that are mostly correct and can discriminate real bugs; Daikon-inferred postconditions rarely discriminate bugs.
cite_claim: GPT-4 produced a test-set-correct postcondition for 96% (158/164) of EvalPlus problems; bug-discriminating postconditions for 70 buggy methods from 64 unique Defects4J bugs (12.2% of 525); only three Daikon postconditions were bug-discriminating, two of which overfit the regression tests.
quote: we observed only three instances of a Daikon-generated postcondition that is bug-discriminating
relevance: Main evidence for adding an intent (tool-description) channel to fiks inference. Trace-only mining encodes current behavior. LLM postconditions from descriptions can encode intended behavior, such as price in dollars.

title: SpecGen: Automated Generation of Formal Program Specifications via Large Language Models
authors: Lezhi Ma, Shangqing Liu, Yi Li, Xiaofei Xie, Lei Bu
central_claim: Conversational LLM generation plus mutation of failing candidates, filtered by a verifier, yields verifiable JML specifications, outperforming Houdini and Daikon.
cite_claim: SpecGen generated verifiable specifications for 279 of 385 programs, outperforming LLM baselines and Houdini/Daikon.
quote: succeeds in generating verifiable specifications for 279 out of 385 programs
relevance: Generate-then-check with a checker in the loop is the pattern to copy. fiks's checker is v1 traffic (falsification) instead of a verifier.

title: Enchanting Program Specification Synthesis by Large Language Models using Static Analysis and Program Verification (AutoSpec)
authors: Cheng Wen, Jialun Cao, Jie Su, Zhiwu Xu, Shengchao Qin, Mengda He, Haokun Li, Shing-Chi Cheung, Cong Tian
central_claim: Static analysis decomposes programs and a verifier validates LLM-proposed specifications per component.
cite_claim: AutoSpec verified 79% of benchmark programs, 1.592x prior work.
quote: outperforms existing works by successfully verifying 79% of programs through automatic specification synthesis
relevance: Further evidence that LLM spec generation needs an external validator. It is relevant to inferring contracts from the MCP server source (white-box) rather than traffic. [verify full author list and venue]

title: Can Large Language Models Reason About Program Invariants?
authors: Kexin Pei, David Bieber, Kensen Shi, Charles Sutton, Pengcheng Yin
central_claim: Fine-tuned code LLMs predict Daikon-style invariants statically, with quality comparable to dynamic analysis given five traces.
cite_claim: Static LLM invariant prediction with a scratchpad matches a dynamic tool with access to five program traces.
quote: quality comparable to those obtained by a dynamic analysis tool with access to five program traces
relevance: Suggests LLM priors can stand in for traffic when v1 samples are scarce (fiks has ~10 fixtures plus 37 bench calls). It is a baseline for the few-trace regime.

title: Do LLMs generate test oracles that capture the actual or the expected program behaviour?
authors: Michael Konstantinou, Renzo Degiovanni, Mike Papadakis
central_claim: LLM-generated oracles, like EvoSuite/Randoop oracles, mostly encode actual rather than expected behavior.
cite_claim: On 24 Java repositories, LLM-based test generation mainly captures actual program behavior, making bug detection difficult; LLMs generate better than they classify oracles.
quote: LLM-based test generation approaches mainly capture the actual program behavior making bug detection difficult
relevance: The reason inferred-from-v1 contracts are regression oracles. They flag change, not wrongness. A reviewer will raise this against automatic fiks contracts.

title: Do LLMs Generate Useful Test Oracles? An Empirical Study with an Unbiased Dataset
authors: Davide Molinelli, Luca Di Grazia, Alberto Martin-Lopez, Michael D. Ernst, Mauro Pezze
central_claim: On 13,866 post-cutoff oracles from 135 Java projects, LLM oracles reach mutation scores comparable to human oracles; complex oracles remain hard.
cite_claim: Prior LLM-oracle studies on Defects4J risk training-data contamination; the post-cutoff dataset avoids it.
quote: created after the cut-off dates of the training of the LLMs used in the experiments
relevance: A methodological rule fiks's evaluation must follow: any LLM-proposed contract evaluated on public APIs or bugs must control for leakage, for example by using our own post-cutoff mock vendor or post-cutoff real bugs.

title: Neural-Based Test Oracle Generation: A Large-scale Evaluation and Lessons Learned
authors: Soneya Binta Hossain, Antonio Filieri, Matthew B. Dwyer, Sebastian Elbaum, Willem Visser
central_claim: Re-evaluating TOGA at scale finds high false-positive assertion oracles and little added fault detection.
cite_claim: Over 47% of TOGA's generated assertion oracles are false positives (abstract); the original TOGA reported 57 Defects4J bugs, and the replication attributes most of those detections to the generated test prefixes rather than TOGA's oracles [verify the 19/57 figure in the full text].
quote: more than 47% of them are false positives
relevance: The strongest critique genre for any oracle-generation claim. fiks must publish per-check FP rates on clean traffic and attribute each detection to a specific inferred property, not to the harness.

title: The Daikon system for dynamic detection of likely invariants
authors: Michael D. Ernst, Jeff H. Perkins, Philip J. Guo, Stephen McCamant, Carlos Pacheco, Matthew S. Tschantz, Chen Xiao
central_claim: Dynamic invariant detection reports properties that held over observed executions, from a template grammar (constants, ranges, linear relations, ordering, containment, sortedness).
cite_claim: Daikon instantiates invariant templates over observed values and reports those true over all observed executions.
quote: Dynamic invariant detection runs a program, observes the values that the program computes, and then reports properties that were true over the observed executions.
relevance: The foundational algorithm. fiks's range/notNull/countMatchesTotal/unique/equalsUpstream kinds are a subset of Daikon's grammar, applied at the tool-result level.

title: Daikon Invariant Detector User Manual
authors: Daikon developers (UW PLSE)
central_claim: Daikon justifies each invariant statistically: it is output only if the probability it held by chance is below a confidence limit; invariants ever falsified are never output; redundant implied invariants are suppressed.
cite_claim: --conf_limit defaults to .99; for a<b, confidence is 1 - 1/2^n, so 3 agreeing samples (.875) are filtered and 9 (.998) pass.
quote: filters out invariants that are satisfied purely by chance
relevance: A concrete, citable justification rule fiks's inferer can adopt to decide the minimum number of v1 observations per template.

title: DIG: A Dynamic Invariant Generator for Polynomial and Array Invariants
authors: ThanhVu Nguyen, Deepak Kapur, Westley Weimer, Stephanie Forrest
central_claim: Generative inference of nonlinear (in)equalities from traces via equation solving and polyhedra, instead of filtering fixed templates.
cite_claim: DIG infers invariants directly from traces rather than filtering predefined templates; evaluated on 27 mathematical algorithms and AES.
quote: infers invariants directly from traces, instead of using traces to filter out predefined templates
relevance: Generative relation inference (e.g. total = sum(qty*price)) would extend fiks beyond fixed templates to cross-field arithmetic. This is relevant to the out-of-vocabulary gap (C11).

title: Investigating Program Behavior Using the Texada LTL Specifications Miner (tool paper; method in 'General LTL Specification Mining', ASE 2015)
authors: Caroline Lemieux, Ivan Beschastnikh (tool demo); Lemieux, Dennis Park, Beschastnikh (ASE 2015)
central_claim: Mines instances of arbitrary user-defined LTL property templates from logs, reporting support and confidence so imperfect traces can be handled.
cite_claim: Texada takes a property-type template (e.g. 'x always precedes y') and a log, and outputs property instances with support, support potential and confidence.
quote: a tool to dynamically mine temporal specifications in LTL from traces of program activity
relevance: The algorithm for mining fiks read-after-write and call-order postconditions (create_order then get_order returns the same id) from v1 call sequences, with support/confidence thresholds.

title: Fuzzing Class Specifications (SpecFuzzer)
authors: Facundo Molina, Marcelo d'Amorim, Nazareno Aguirre
central_claim: Grammar-based fuzzing generates candidate assertions, Daikon filters those falsified by tests, and mutation analysis clusters and ranks the survivors.
cite_claim: SpecFuzzer uses a fuzzer as a generator of candidate assertions, Daikon to filter out assertions invalidated by a test suite, and mutation analysis to cluster and rank the survivors; it is reported more effective than GAssert and EvoSpex on 43 Java methods.
location: Abstract; evaluation (43 methods, per search summary [verify count])
quote: a novel technique that combines grammar-based fuzzing, dynamic invariant detection, and mutation analysis
relevance: Design pattern for fiks: over-generate candidate contracts, falsify on v1 traffic, then rank by how many seeded upstream mutants each kills. Mind the miner/injector alignment risk.

title: A comparative study of programmer-written and automatically inferred contracts
authors: Nadia Polikarpova, Ilinca Ciupa, Bertrand Meyer
central_claim: Daikon infers about five times as many relevant clauses as programmers write but recovers only ~60% of programmer contracts; about a third of inferred clauses are incorrect or irrelevant.
cite_claim: On 25 classes with over 19,500 inferred clauses: ~5x as many relevant clauses as programmers, ~60% of programmer-written contracts recovered, ~1/3 of inferred clauses incorrect or irrelevant.
quote: Around a third of the generated assertions clauses are either incorrect or irrelevant.
relevance: The baseline expectation for comparing fiks inferred contracts with hand-written ones (an experiment the codebase map proposes). Expect high volume, partial recall and needed pruning.

title: Understanding user understanding: determining correctness of generated program invariants
authors: Matt Staats, Shin Hong, Moonzoo Kim, Gregg Rothermel
central_claim: Humans asked to classify generated invariants as correct or incorrect make frequent errors, undermining human-in-the-loop invariant vetting.
cite_claim: 30 participants misclassified 9.1%-31.7% of correct invariants and 26.1%-58.6% of incorrect invariants.
location: Abstract (as reproduced by the ORBilu record; PDF link 404 on 2026-10-21) [verify]
quote: misclassified 9.1% to 31.7% of correct invariants and 26.1%-58.6% of incorrect invariants [verify exact wording]
relevance: Undercuts the 'a developer reviews the inferred contracts' escape hatch used by AGORA+, Deequ and Lisa. fiks should measure inferred-contract FP automatically on held-out clean traffic, not rely on review.

title: Automatically patching errors in deployed software (ClearView)
authors: Jeff H. Perkins, Sunghun Kim, Sam Larsen, Saman Amarasinghe, et al., Michael D. Ernst, Martin Rinard
central_claim: Learn invariants from normal runs, detect failures, find invariants violated in failing runs, generate patches that re-establish them, and pick the best by observing patched runs.
cite_claim: ClearView blocked all 10 Red Team exploits and auto-generated patches correcting the error for 7 of 10, on stripped x86 binaries.
quote: ClearView (1) observes normal executions to learn invariants that characterize the application's normal behavior
relevance: The most important precedent for fiks's whole loop (learned invariants, then violation, then patch). Novelty claims must differentiate it: ClearView patches binaries at runtime against security failures with learned invariants, while fiks produces a source-level PR with a reproduction test and CI gates for semantic tool-output faults.

title: Mining Invariants from Console Logs for System Problem Detection
authors: Jian-Guang Lou, Qiang Fu, Shengqi Yang, Ye Xu, Jiang Li
central_claim: Linear count invariants mined from parsed logs (e.g. count(JVM spawned) = count(JVM exited)) detect anomalies with interpretable explanations.
cite_claim: On ~24M Hadoop log lines no false-positive invariant was found, yet the alarms still included false positives: 1777 from killed speculative tasks and 778 from job setup/cleanup tasks. The authors argue the number of FP types matters more than the count.
quote: No false positive invariant is found.
relevance: Shows that a correct invariant can still raise false alarms on legitimate rare behavior. Count invariants match fiks countMatchesTotal (D4). FP 'types' maps onto deduplicating fiks receipts by property id.

title: Log-based Anomaly Detection with Deep Learning: How Far Are We?
authors: Van-Hoang Le, Hongyu Zhang
central_claim: Reported F>0.9 for deep log anomaly detectors does not survive changes in training-data selection, grouping, class distribution, noise and early detection.
cite_claim: Training data selection, data grouping, class distribution, data noise and early detection all have significant impact on the evaluation of five deep log anomaly detectors on four datasets.
quote: The problem of log-based anomaly detection has not been solved yet.
relevance: Critique for learned statistical anomaly detectors as a fiks alternative or baseline. Any learned detector must be evaluated with chronological splits and realistic class balance.

title: Automating Large-Scale Data Quality Verification (Deequ)
authors: Sebastian Schelter, Dustin Lange, Philipp Schmidt, Meltem Celikel, Felix Biessmann, Andreas Grafberger
central_claim: Declarative 'unit tests for data' plus heuristic constraint suggestion from column profiles (isComplete, hasCompleteness with CI lower bound, hasConsistentType, isUnique via HLL, range compliance, categorical isInRange), with ML to vet uniqueness.
cite_claim: Suggesting on a 10% sample and checking on the other 90%: all reddit constraints held; on twitter users two failed (a categorical lang domain missing rare values; a spurious isUnique on statuses_count, 64% unique), the latter fixed by a column-name classifier.
quote: rely on the end user to select from and validate our suggestions which might not necessarily hold for future data
relevance: Directly implementable heuristics that map onto fiks kinds (notNull, range, unique, categorical). Its 10/90 held-out coverage protocol is a ready FP methodology. It also documents categorical domains and uniqueness as FP-prone. Deequ/PyDeequ are open source (Apache-2.0 [verify license]).

title: Data Validation for Machine Learning
authors: Eric Breck, Neoklis Polyzotis, Sudip Roy, Steven Euijong Whang, Martin Zinkevich
central_claim: A production data-validation system (TFX/TFDV) infers a schema from data statistics, validates new data against it, and detects training/serving skew; deployed across Google.
cite_claim: Google's data validation system detects anomalies in data fed to ML pipelines and monitors petabytes of production data daily; TFDV's infer_schema bootstraps a schema that developers then refine.
quote: a data validation system that is designed to detect anomalies specifically in data fed into machine learning pipelines
relevance: Industrial precedent for 'infer schema from v1, validate v2, human curates': the TFDV workflow is a runnable baseline (Apache-2.0) on flattened tool outputs. [verify author list order]

title: Reducing Ambiguity in Json Schema Discovery (Jxplain)
authors: William Spoth, Oliver Kennedy, Ying Lu, Beda Hammerschmidt, Zhen Hua Liu
central_claim: Existing JSON schema discovery makes data-independent assumptions that APIs violate (e.g. object-as-map vs record), producing imprecise schemas and validation false positives; Jxplain's heuristics yield more precise schemas.
cite_claim: Schema discovery tools produce imprecise schemas on API data, creating many opportunities for false positives during validation.
quote: When these assumptions are violated, most notably by APIs, the generated schemas are imprecise, creating numerous opportunities for false positives during validation.
relevance: Inferring outputSchema from v1 samples is the cheapest baseline (schema-only, C4/C26). Jxplain shows naive inference is FP-prone on API JSON (dynamic keys), which affects the inferred-schema baseline's FP rate.

title: Diffy: find potential bugs in services using side-by-side regression testing
authors: Twitter (Puneet Khanduri et al.)
central_claim: Proxy multicasts each request to candidate, primary and secondary instances; primary vs secondary disagreement estimates non-deterministic noise that is cancelled when judging candidate vs primary.
cite_claim: Diffy treats differences between two instances of the same known-good code as noise and ignores fields whose candidate-vs-primary difference rate matches that noise.
quote: Non-deterministic noise observed between the primary and secondary instances.
relevance: A concrete, cheap noise-field detector for fiks inference: replay each v1 call twice and exclude fields that differ (ids, timestamps) from equality/categorical invariants. Also the strongest 'just diff old vs new' baseline, which needs a live old version that third-party vendors do not provide.

title: mitmproxy2swagger: automatically convert mitmproxy captures to OpenAPI 3.0 specifications
authors: alufers and contributors
central_claim: Infers an OpenAPI spec (paths, schemas, examples) from captured HTTP traffic or HAR files in a two-pass curated workflow.
cite_claim: Traffic-to-OpenAPI inference exists as an engineering tool; it produces structural schemas, not semantic invariants.
quote: Automagically reverse-engineer REST APIs via capturing traffic
relevance: Practitioner baseline: infer the upstream spec from v1 tap traffic and then spec-diff on v2 (C27). It cannot see D1/D5 because types are unchanged, which shows why semantic invariants are needed. License: MIT.
